claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: K14cre-HIF-2α mice and K14cre-NOS2 mutants exhibit a constitutive hypotensive state.
claims.source: Continuous monitoring of unrestrained, non-anesthetised mice via radio-telemetric catheterization showed that although resting heart rates were unchanged in all mutants relative to wild type controls (n = 7) through diurnal variation (Figure 1A), there was a constitutive hypotensive state in K14cre-HIF-2α mice (n = 7) and NOS2 mutants (n = 6) (Figure 1B) and a strong trend towards a hypertensive state in K14cre-HIF-1α mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: K14cre-HIF-1α mice show a strong trend towards a hypertensive state.
claims.source: Continuous monitoring of unrestrained, non-anesthetised mice via radio-telemetric catheterization showed that although resting heart rates were unchanged in all mutants relative to wild type controls (n = 7) through diurnal variation (Figure 1A), there was a constitutive hypotensive state in K14cre-HIF-2α mice (n = 7) and NOS2 mutants (n = 6) (Figure 1B) and a strong trend towards a hypertensive state in K14cre-HIF-1α mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Cutaneous temperatures in K14cre-Arg-1 mutants are significantly higher than littermate controls.
claims.source: Cutaneous temperatures were also monitored by radiotelemetry (Figure 1C). Here, we saw that cutaneous temperatures in K14cre-Arg-1 mutants was significantly higher than littermate controls and trend lower in HIF-1α mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Cutaneous temperatures in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants trend lower than littermate controls.
claims.source: Cutaneous temperatures were also monitored by radiotelemetry (Figure 1C). Here, we saw that cutaneous temperatures in K14cre-Arg-1 mutants was significantly higher than littermate controls and trend lower in HIF-1α mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference in physical activity between mutant groups and littermate control mice.
claims.source: Analysis of physical activity showed no significant difference in the movement levels between the mutant groups and littermate control mice, suggesting these differences in temperature do not result from variable activity (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Differences in skin temperature between mutants and controls do not result from variable activity.
claims.source: Analysis of physical activity showed no significant difference in the movement levels between the mutant groups and littermate control mice, suggesting these differences in temperature do not result from variable activity (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the activity data presented in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: There is an acute cardiovascular response to hypoxia in the first 10-15 min with increased ventilation and a hypoxic pressor reflex.
claims.source: As noted above, the acute cardiovascular response to hypoxia has been described in a number of animal models. As previous investigators have documented, there was an acute response in the first 10–15 min, with increased ventilation (160BrPM to 250BrPM), and a hypoxic pressor reflex, with blood pressures increasing from means of 123/88 mmHg (baseline) to 143/102 mmHg within the first 10 min (Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B and citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Following the initial response to hypoxia, there is a severe drop in systemic blood pressures at 12% and 10% oxygen levels.
claims.source: Following this brief initial response, there was a severe drop in systemic blood pressures at the 12% and 10% oxygen levels, to means of 87 mmHg SBP and 57 mmHg DBP at 120 min for 10% oxygen (Figure 2C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claims.claim: Heart rates peak at 13 min in the lowest level of hypoxia, from 606 BPM to 717 BPM, followed by a decline to 285 BPM at 120 min post-transition.
claims.source: Heart rates peak at 13 min in the lowest level of hypoxia, from 606 BPM (baseline) to 717 BPM at the lowest levels of oxygen, followed immediately by a decline to 285 BPM (a 53% drop from baseline) at 120 min post-transition (Figure 2E–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claims.claim: Skin temperature rapidly decreased from 33.7°C to 28.9°C 180 mins post hypoxic challenge, suggesting an increase in peripheral vascular resistance.
claims.source: Analysis of subcutaneous temperature has previously been used as an indirect measurement of peripheral vascular resistance(Schey et al., 2009). We found that skin temperature rapidly decreased from 33.7°C (baseline) to 28.9°C (−4.8°C) 180mins post hypoxic challenge (Figure 2G), suggesting an increase in peripheral vascular resistance.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and inference based on cited methodology.

claims.claim: Physical activity declined from 5.3 m/hr to 0.2 m/hr in the 120 min following the introduction of 10% oxygen.
claims.source: Physical activity also declined from 5.3 m/hr to 0.2 m/hr in the 120 min following the introduction of 10% oxygen.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: At 10% oxygen, recovery to 90% of normoxic heart rates and blood pressures occurred in 36 hr in wild type controls.
claims.source: We defined recovery as the point at which the animal reached 90% of heart rates and blood pressures seen at the same time of the diurnal cycle in normoxia; with this definition, recovery occured in 36 hr at 10% oxygen levels in wild type controls.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and the authors' definition of recovery.

claims.claim: The onset of 10% environmental hypoxia causes a sharper drop in skin temperatures in K14cre-HIF-1α mice than in littermate control animals.
claims.source: As described above and shown in Figure 1, there is a decrease in skin temperature in mice lacking HIF-1α in keratinocytes. In these mice, the onset of 10% environmental hypoxia causes a sharper drop in skin temperatures (Figure 3A) than that seen in littermate control animals, and temperatures of the skin in HIF-1α mutants remain well below those of littermate mice in the second phase of hypoxic response; they do not recover until the restoration of normoxia (for statistical analysis see Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Skin temperatures in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants remain well below those of littermate mice in the second phase of hypoxic response and do not recover until the restoration of normoxia.
claims.source: As described above and shown in Figure 1, there is a decrease in skin temperature in mice lacking HIF-1α in keratinocytes. In these mice, the onset of 10% environmental hypoxia causes a sharper drop in skin temperatures (Figure 3A) than that seen in littermate control animals, and temperatures of the skin in HIF-1α mutants remain well below those of littermate mice in the second phase of hypoxic response; they do not recover until the restoration of normoxia (for statistical analysis see Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The initial drop in skin temperature during hypoxia is comparable between K14cre-HIF-1α mutant and littermate control mice as shown by infra-red analysis.
claims.source: Infra-red analysis of skin temperature was also used to monitor peripheral vascular perfusion during hypoxic challenge. The initial drop in skin temperature was comparable between K14cre-HIF-1α mutant and littermate control mice, as shown in Figure 3B.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: K14cre-HIF-1α mutants are essentially hypertensive under normoxic conditions, and this hypertension is exaggerated in the first phase of hypoxic response.
claims.source: As described above, the HIF-1α mutants are essentially hypertensive under normoxic conditions, and this hypertension is exaggerated in the first phase of hypoxic response (Figure 3C, for statistical analysis see Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 9B.

claims.claim: In the second phase of hypoxia, K14cre-HIF-1α mutants show a larger drop in systolic and diastolic pressures relative to littermate control mice.
claims.source: However, in the second phase there is a larger drop in systolic and diastolic pressures relative to littermate control mice (Figure 3D, for statistical analysis see Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 9C.

claims.claim: Diastolic pressures in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants begin to elevate in the first hour of hypoxia and gradually increase throughout the 48 hr of hypoxic exposure.
claims.source: This resolves rapidly, and although the subsequent systolic pressures in mutants are similar to those in littermate control animals, the diastolic pressures in the mutants begin to elevate. This elevated diastolic pressure begins in the first hour of hypoxia, and gradually increases throughout the 48 hr of hypoxic exposure (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Elevation of systolic pressures in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants does not reappear until the animals are restored to normoxia.
claims.source: An elevation in systolic pressures in HIF-1α mutants does not reappear until the animals are restored to normoxia.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Elevation of diastolic pressures is indicative of an increase in peripheral resistance.
claims.source: Elevation of diastolic pressures is indicative of an increase in peripheral resistance, and this is consistent with the lowered skin temperatures described above (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on established physiological knowledge and consistency with observed data.

claims.claim: K14cre-HIF-1α mutants show an increase in heart rate that is likely required to sustain systolic pressures, coinciding with the relative increase in diastolic pressures.
claims.source: In Figure 3E and F, the acute and chronic changes in heart rate in littermate control and mutant animals can be seen (for statistical analysis see Figure 9D and E). The chief difference seen in the HIF-1α mutants is an increase in heart rate that is likely required to sustain systolic pressures; this coincides with the relative increase in diastolic pressures in HIF-1α mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-F and Figure 9D-E, with inference about the physiological mechanism.

claims.claim: The chronic change in heart rate in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants appears to coincide with an increase in whole-body metabolic activity between 12-36 hr hypoxia.
claims.source: The chronic change in heart rate in HIF-1α mutants appears to coincide with an increase in whole-body metabolic activity between 12–36 hr hypoxia, as determined by VO2 and VCO2 analysis (Figure 3G and H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claims.claim: Normal metabolic activity in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants is only restored when the animals are returned to normoxia.
claims.source: Normal metabolic activity is only restored when the animals are returned to normoxia.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Physical activity is reduced in littermate control and K14cre-HIF-1α mutant animals during the initial 12 hr of hypoxia.
claims.source: Physical activity is reduced in littermate control and mutant animals during the initial 12 hr of hypoxia. Activity slowly increases during the acclimation period, but does not fully recover until the animals are restored to normoxia (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H (note: text refers to Figure 3H but likely means 3I based on figure layout).

claims.claim: Loss of HIF-1α in the epidermis delays the cardiovascular changes that occur in response to hypoxia, correlated with an increase in peripheral resistance and heart rates.
claims.source: Overall, loss of HIF-1α in the epidermis appears to delay the cardiovascular changes that occur in response to hypoxia; this is correlated with an increase in peripheral resistance and in heart rates.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Hypoxia results in an initial HIF-1α/NOS2/NO mediated increase in vascular diameter and resulting increases in perfusion, followed by a HIF-2α/Arginase-induced reduction of intracellular L-arginine that suppresses NO production and causes vasoconstriction.
claims.source: We have proposed a model for hypoxic responses involving HIF isoform activity and nitric oxide homeostasis in the skin that argues that hypoxia results in an initial HIF-1α/NOS2/NO mediated increase in vascular diameter, and resulting increases in perfusion; followed by a HIF-2α/Arginase-induced reduction of intracellular L-arginine (Cowburn et al., 2013). As L-arginine is necessary for NO production, this would suppress NO production by NO synthases, and ultimately cause vasoconstriction.
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on previous research and current findings.

claims.claim: Animals lacking HIF-2α in the epidermis show elevated skin temperatures in the first 12 hr of hypoxia relative to littermate control animals.
claims.source: This model for HIFα isoform action in hypoxic vascular tissues fits the observations described above for the loss of HIF-1α in the skin. In animals lacking HIF-2α in the epidermis, adaptation of skin temperatures in the first 12 hr of hypoxia follows the predictions of this model (Figure 4A), that is, we see elevated skin temperatures in the HIF-2α mutants relative to littermate control animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Infra-red analysis shows that the recorded drop in skin temperature during hypoxia is significantly less in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants relative to littermate control animals.
claims.source: These data are supported by infra-red analysis of skin temperature during short term hypoxia exposure (Figure 4B). The recorded drop in skin temperature is significantly less in the HIF-2α mutants relative to littermate control animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: After 24 hr of hypoxia, skin temperatures in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants drop relative to littermate control animals and remain lower for 12 hr before rising again to levels similar to littermate controls.
claims.source: However, after 24 hr, skin temperatures in mutants drop relative to littermate control animals, and remain lower than those of littermate control animals for 12 hr, before rising again to levels similar to those of littermate controls.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Upon restoration of environmental normoxia, skin temperatures in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants return to levels slightly higher than those seen in littermate control animals.
claims.source: Upon restoration of environmental normoxia, skin temperatures in mutants return to levels slightly higher than those seen in littermate control animals, that is, similar to those seen at steady state (for statistical analysis see Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claims.claim: For the first 24 hr of hypoxia, K14cre-HIF-2α mutants show elevated systolic and diastolic pressures that are evident in the first minutes of hypoxic exposure.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1, mean blood pressures of HIF-2α mutants are significantly lower than those of littermate control animals. For the first 24 hr of hypoxia, HIF-2α mutants show elevated systolic and diastolic pressures that are evident in the first minutes of hypoxic exposure (Figure 4C, [for statistical analysis see Figure 9G] and Figure 4D, [for statistical analysis see Figure 9H]).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D and Figure 9G-H.

claims.claim: At 24 hr of hypoxia, diastolic pressures in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants are similar to those seen in littermate control animals, but systolic pressure drops relative to littermate controls.
claims.source: Here again, there is a shift at 24 hr, and although diastolic pressures at that point are similar to those seen in littermate control animals, systolic pressure drops relative to littermate controls.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Systolic blood pressures in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants remain substantially lower than littermate controls until normoxia is restored.
claims.source: The systolic blood pressures remain substantially lower until normoxia is restored, when they return to steady state and mildly hypotensive levels.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: At the return of normoxia, diastolic pressures in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants rise to levels substantially higher than those seen in littermate control animals for approximately 12 hr.
claims.source: Finally, at the return of normoxia, diastolic pressures rise to levels substantially higher than those seen in littermate control animals for approximately 12 hr, before finally dropping again 24 hr after the restoration of normoxia.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Changes in the skin affect both traditionally understood changes in peripheral resistance (altered diastolic pressures) and other changes that can influence systolic pressures.
claims.source: This effect on both systolic and diastolic pressures indicates that changes in the skin affect both traditionally understood changes in peripheral resistance, that is, changes that result in altered diastolic pressures, and other changes that can influence systolic pressures.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on blood pressure changes.

claims.claim: Hypoxia has virtually no effect on heart rate in K14cre-HIF-2α mutant animals.
claims.source: The effect of hypoxia on the heart rate of the epidermal HIF-2α knockout animals is strikingly altered when compared to the effect on littermate control animals. Hypoxia has virtually no effect on heart rate in the HIF-2α mutant animals (Figure 4E, for statistical analysis see Figure 9I); they show a diurnal variation of heart rate that is essentially the same as that seen in animals in normoxic conditions (Figure 4F, for statistical analysis see Figure 9J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-F and Figure 9I-J.

claims.claim: K14cre-HIF-2α mutant animals show a diurnal variation of heart rate that is essentially the same as that seen in animals in normoxic conditions.
claims.source: The effect of hypoxia on the heart rate of the epidermal HIF-2α knockout animals is strikingly altered when compared to the effect on littermate control animals. Hypoxia has virtually no effect on heart rate in the HIF-2α mutant animals (Figure 4E, for statistical analysis see Figure 9I); they show a diurnal variation of heart rate that is essentially the same as that seen in animals in normoxic conditions (Figure 4F, for statistical analysis see Figure 9J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-F and Figure 9I-J.

claims.claim: Whole-body metabolic activity (VO2 and VCO2) in K14cre-HIF-2α mutant animals is significantly increased above littermate control rates between 12-24 hr hypoxia.
claims.source: Whole-body metabolic activity (VO2 and VCO2) in HIF-2α mutant animals is also significantly increased above littermate control rates between 12–24 hr hypoxia (Figure 4G and H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claims.claim: Increased metabolic activity in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants does not return to levels seen in littermate control animals until the mice are returned to normoxia.
claims.source: This increased metabolic activity does not return to levels seen in littermate control animals until the mice are returned to normoxia.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Activity of K14cre-HIF-2α mutant animals recovers substantially between 12-48 hr of hypoxia, although it does not fully recover until the animals are restored to normoxia.
claims.source: Physical activity, similarly to the patterns described above, is greatly reduced in littermate and mutant animals during the initial 12 hr of hypoxia. However, activity of HIF-2α mutant animals recovers substantially between 12–48 hr, although it does not fully recover until the animals are restored to normoxia (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: The crossover seen in skin temperature and blood pressure at 24 hr indicates a phase of adaptation revealed by the HIF-2α deletion, related to a temporally specific action of HIF-2α in the adaptation and response to hypoxia.
claims.source: These results indicate a complex response of the skin to systemic hypoxia, and also demonstrate that that complexity is mirrored in the effect of those responses on the cardiovascular system. The crossover seen in skin temperature and blood pressure at 24 hr also indicates that there is likely a phase of adaptation at that time point revealed by the HIF-2α deletion, and related to a temporally specific action of HIF-2α in the adaptation and response to hypoxia.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on temporal patterns.

claims.claim: There is a steep drop in plasma NO metabolites over the first day of hypoxia, followed by a more gradual decline over the following 3 days of exposure.
claims.source: Given the complex role of HIF-2α in the epidermis, and our hypothesis that this could be determined by the differential effect of HIF-1α and HIF-2α on NO homeostasis, we next analysed the overall levels of NO metabolites induced by hypoxia in specific tissues following hypoxic exposure (Figure 5). As can be seen in Figure 5A, there was a steep drop in plasma NO metabolites over the first day of hypoxia, followed by a more gradual decline over the following 3 days of exposure (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Skin shows an initial spike in arginase-1 and -2 expression in the first 24 hr of hypoxia exposure, which then declines.
claims.source: However, as shown in Figure 5B, in skin, and in Figure 5C, in lungs, differing levels of expression of hypoxia-sensitive genes involved in the NO synthesis pathway are evident. Of note, the skin shows an initial spike in arginase-1 and -2 expression in the first 24 hr of exposure, which then declines.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Skin NOS2 expression is marginally higher during the first 24 hr of hypoxia.
claims.source: Skin NOS2 expression over the same time is marginally higher, however.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: In the lung, there is no substantial increase in NOS2 or arginase-1 or -2 expression until after two days of exposure to hypoxia.
claims.source: In the lung there is no substantial increase in NOS2 or arginase-1 or -2 expression until after two days of exposure to hypoxia.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The levels of NO metabolites in the skin and lung reflect the expression levels of arginase and NOS2 mRNA.
claims.source: The levels of NO metabolites seen in the skin and lung reflect the expression levels of arginase and NOS2 mRNA, with an increase seen in the skin at 24 hr and a subsequent decline to baseline levels after 2 days of hypoxia (Figure 5D). This is in contrast to the lung, which shows a gradual decline in NO metabolites at 48–72 hr (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claims.claim: Skin shows an increase in NO metabolites at 24 hr and a subsequent decline to baseline levels after 2 days of hypoxia.
claims.source: The levels of NO metabolites seen in the skin and lung reflect the expression levels of arginase and NOS2 mRNA, with an increase seen in the skin at 24 hr and a subsequent decline to baseline levels after 2 days of hypoxia (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The lung shows a gradual decline in NO metabolites at 48-72 hr of hypoxia.
claims.source: This is in contrast to the lung, which shows a gradual decline in NO metabolites at 48–72 hr (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: There is a temporal and tissue-specific shift in the expression of NOS2 and Arg-1/-2 in vivo.
claims.source: These data indicate a temporal and tissue-specific shift in the expression of NOS2 and Arg-1/-2 in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on gene expression patterns.

claims.claim: Deletion efficiency of epidermal NOS2 in K14cre+ mice is greater than 98%.
claims.source: To test the hypothesis that keratinocyte HIF-1α/NOS/NO influences shifts in skin temperature, systemic blood pressure and heart rates during exposure to hypoxia, we next generated mice with NOS2 deletions in keratinocytes. Deletion efficiency of epidermal NOS2 in K14cre+ mice was calculated to be greater than 98% in all mice analysed (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Deletion of epidermal NOS2 shows changes in baseline skin temperature and systemic blood pressures similar to those seen in HIF-2α mutant mice.
claims.source: The deletion of epidermal NOS2 shows changes in baseline skin temperature (which is likely correlated with peripheral vascular resistance) and systemic blood pressures similar to those seen in HIF-2α mutant mice, and initial changes in heart rate similar to those seen in HIF-1α mutant mice.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data across different mutant lines.

claims.claim: Deletion of epidermal NOS2 shows initial changes in heart rate similar to those seen in HIF-1α mutant mice.
claims.source: The deletion of epidermal NOS2 shows changes in baseline skin temperature (which is likely correlated with peripheral vascular resistance) and systemic blood pressures similar to those seen in HIF-2α mutant mice, and initial changes in heart rate similar to those seen in HIF-1α mutant mice.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data across different mutant lines.

claims.claim: Epidermal deletion of NOS2 sustains an elevated skin temperature relative to littermate controls for the first 24 hr of hypoxia.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6A, epidermal deletion of NOS2 sustains an elevated skin temperature relative to littermate controls for the first 24 hr of hypoxia, before returning to levels seen in control mice for the remainder of the recording (for statistical analysis see Figure 9K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 9K.

claims.claim: K14cre-NOS2 mutant animals display a profound hypotensive phenotype with an apparent decrease in both systolic and diastolic pressures within the first 20 min of hypoxia exposure.
claims.source: In Figure 6C and D, the similarities to the HIF-2α mutant mice are evident, as the K14-NOS2 mutant animals display a profound hypotensive phenotype, with an apparent decrease in both systolic and diastolic pressures within the first 20 min of hypoxia exposure (for statistical analysis see Figure 9L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-D and Figure 9L.

claims.claim: The hypotensive state in K14cre-NOS2 mutants is maintained throughout the hypoxic time course.
claims.source: This hypotensive state is maintained throughout the hypoxic time course (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Maximal deflection of systolic pressures (-15 to -20 mmHg) in K14cre-NOS2 mutants occurs between 24-48 hr hypoxic exposure when compared to littermate controls.
claims.source: Maximal deflection of systolic pressures (−15 to −20 mmHg) occurs between 24–48 hr hypoxic exposure when compared to littermate controls (statistical analysis Figure 9M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 9M.

claims.claim: K14cre-NOS2 mutant heart rate acclimation to hypoxia responds in a similar pattern to HIF-1α mutants, with a profound increase in BPM 120 mins after hypoxia exposure that is maintained throughout the first 24 hr.
claims.source: In contrast, NOS2 mutant heart rate acclimation to hypoxia responds in a similar pattern to the HIF-1α mutants, with a profound increase in BPM 120mins after hypoxia exposure. This is also maintained throughout the first 24 hr of hypoxia exposure (Figure 6E and F [for statistical analysis see Figure 9N and O]).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-F and Figure 9N-O.

claims.claim: RT-qPCR analysis identified a significant increase in the expression of both NOS1 and NOS3 in K14cre-NOS2 mice exposed to hypoxia when compared to littermate controls.
claims.source: The distinct tensive/cardiac response to hypoxia reported above may be due to a potential compensatory role of NOS1 and NOS3 expression in the skin counteracting the loss of NOS2. RT-qPCR analysis in whole skin samples identified a significant increase in the expression of both NOS1 and NOS3 in K14cre-NOS2 mice exposed to hypoxia (6 hr) when compared to littermate controls (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: The compensatory roles of NOS isoform expression have been previously reported in other animal models of NOS deletion.
claims.source: The compensatory roles of NOS isoform expression have been previously reported in other animal models of NOS deletion (Colton et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Comparative analysis of VEGF-A identified no compensatory expression in K14cre-NOS2 mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, comparative analysis of VEGF-A identified no compensatory expression in K14cre-NOS2 mice (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: K14cre-Arg1 mutant animals display an elevated skin temperature relative to littermate control mice during the first twelve hours of hypoxic exposure, followed by a relative decline at 24 hr.
claims.source: To determine if the complex shifts in skin temperature, blood pressure and heart rate during hypoxia seen in HIF-2α mutant animals were due to HIF-2α regulation of the arginase pathway, we next analysed mice with Arg1 deletions in keratinocytes. As can be seen in Figure 7A, and similarly to what was seen in HIF-2α mutant mice, these animals display an elevated skin temperature relative to littermate control mice during the first twelve hours of hypoxic exposure, followed by a relative decline at 24 hr (for statistical analysis see Figure 9P).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 9P.

claims.claim: K14cre-Arg1 mutants show a small increase in systolic and diastolic pressures for the first 10 min of hypoxia, followed by a decrease in both pressures similar to littermate control animals.
claims.source: In Figure 7B (for statistical analysis see Figure 9Q) it is apparent that there is a small increase in systolic and diastolic pressures for the first 10 min hypoxia, followed by a decrease in both systolic and diastolic pressure. This occurs in a manner similar to that of littermate control animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 9Q.

claims.claim: The recovery of a normotensive state in K14cre-Arg1 mutant mice is somewhat similar to that seen in littermate controls.
claims.source: The recovery of a normotensive state in K14cre-Arg1 mutant mice, is somewhat similar to that seen in littermate controls (Figure 7C)(for statistical analysis see Figure 9R).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 9R.

claims.claim: The effect on heart rate in K14cre-Arg1 mutants is similar to that seen in HIF-2α mutants, with an overall increase relative to the hypoxia-induced decline seen in littermate control animals.
claims.source: However, the effect on heart rate is similar in some regards to that seen in HIF-2α mutants, with an overall increase relative to the hypoxia-induced decline seen in littermate control animals (Figure 7D)(for statistical analysis see Figure 9S), and a more rapid return to the normal pattern of diurnal variation in heart rate (Figure 7E)(for statistical analysis see Figure 9T).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D-E and Figure 9S-T.

claims.claim: K14cre-Arg1 mutants show a more rapid return to the normal pattern of diurnal variation in heart rate compared to littermate controls.
claims.source: However, the effect on heart rate is similar in some regards to that seen in HIF-2α mutants, with an overall increase relative to the hypoxia-induced decline seen in littermate control animals (Figure 7D)(for statistical analysis see Figure 9S), and a more rapid return to the normal pattern of diurnal variation in heart rate (Figure 7E)(for statistical analysis see Figure 9T).

results.result: Wild-type mice exhibit a tri-phasic cardiovascular response to hypoxia: an initial 10-minute hypertensive/tachycardic phase, followed by profound hypotension/bradycardia lasting up to 24 hours, then gradual recovery over ~36-45 hours. This response is graded by oxygen level and accompanied by decreased skin temperature and physical activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C19, C29-C34, and C98-C102 collectively describe a novel tri-phasic cardiovascular response pattern supported by radiotelemetry data in Figures 2 and accompanying text. The temporal dynamics, magnitude of changes, and dose-response relationship are well-documented with appropriate controls and statistical analysis (C127). This represents a major advance over previous short-term anesthetized studies.

results.result: Under normoxic conditions, K14cre-HIF-2α and K14cre-NOS2 mutants exhibit constitutive hypotension, K14cre-HIF-1α mutants trend toward hypertension, and K14cre-Arg1 mutants show elevated skin temperature, with no changes in resting heart rate or physical activity across genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C28 describe baseline phenotypes supported by radiotelemetry data in Figure 1. Statistical significance is reported for blood pressure (C23) and skin temperature (C25) changes. The lack of heart rate and activity differences (C22, C27) provides important controls showing specificity of vascular effects. Sample sizes are adequate (n=5-10 per group).

results.result: Loss of epidermal HIF-1α delays cardiovascular adaptation to hypoxia, characterized by exaggerated initial hypertension, sustained elevation of diastolic pressure throughout hypoxia (indicating increased peripheral resistance), compensatory tachycardia, increased metabolic activity, and lower skin temperatures that persist until normoxia is restored.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C47 describe HIF-1α mutant phenotypes supported by extensive radiotelemetry data in Figures 3 and 9A-E. The interpretation linking elevated diastolic pressure to increased peripheral resistance (C42) is physiologically sound and consistent with decreased skin temperature (C35-C36). The compensatory tachycardia (C43) and increased metabolism (C44) represent logical physiological responses. Statistical analysis confirms significant differences (Figure 9).

results.result: Loss of epidermal HIF-2α produces complex biphasic effects on hypoxic adaptation: elevated skin temperature and blood pressure in the first 24 hours, followed by a transition at 24 hours with decreased systolic pressure and skin temperature. Notably, heart rate remains stable throughout hypoxia, showing normal diurnal variation, while metabolic activity and physical activity are better preserved than in controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C63 describe HIF-2α mutant phenotypes supported by data in Figures 4 and 9F-J. The biphasic response with a 24-hour transition point (C51, C54, C63) is clearly documented. The striking preservation of heart rate (C58-C59) and partial preservation of activity (C62) distinguish this phenotype from HIF-1α mutants. The inference about a temporally-specific HIF-2α action (C63) is reasonable given the crossover pattern. Infrared imaging (Figure 4B) provides independent validation of skin temperature changes.

results.result: Hypoxia induces temporal and tissue-specific changes in NO pathway gene expression: skin shows early (24hr) spikes in arginase-1/-2 and modest NOS2 increases with corresponding NO metabolite elevation, while lung shows delayed (48-72hr) increases in these genes with gradual NO metabolite decline. Plasma NO metabolites decline steeply over the first day then more gradually.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C71 describe tissue-specific NO dynamics supported by qPCR and biochemical data in Figure 5. The temporal patterns differ between skin and lung, supporting tissue-specific regulation. NO metabolite levels correlate with gene expression patterns (C68), providing functional validation. Statistical significance is indicated for multiple timepoints. However, the manuscript lacks details on normalization methods and number of biological replicates for some measurements.

results.result: Epidermal NOS2 deletion (>98% efficient) produces a mixed phenotype combining features of both HIF-2α mutants (hypotension, elevated skin temperature in first 24hr) and HIF-1α mutants (compensatory tachycardia). Compensatory upregulation of NOS1 and NOS3 is observed in hypoxia, but not VEGF-A.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C82 describe NOS2 mutant phenotypes supported by data in Figures 6 and 9K-O. High deletion efficiency (C72) is documented by TaqMan PCR. The mixed phenotype (C73-C74) is well-characterized and the compensatory NOS isoform upregulation (C80) provides mechanistic insight, though this complicates interpretation. The lack of VEGF compensation (C82) is an important control. The comparison to prior literature on NOS compensation (C81) strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: Epidermal Arg1 deletion partially phenocopies HIF-2α mutants with elevated early skin temperature, relatively preserved heart rate and activity, and increased metabolism during hypoxia. However, effects are less pronounced than in HIF-2α mutants, suggesting additional HIF-2α target genes contribute to the full phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C90 describe Arg1 mutant phenotypes supported by data in Figures 7 and 9P-T. The partial phenocopy of HIF-2α mutants (C83, C86-C88) supports the hypothesis that arginase mediates some HIF-2α effects. The inference that other HIF-2α targets are involved (C89-C90) is reasonable given the attenuated phenotype, though the presence of Arg2 (C89) is an alternative explanation that should be tested. Blood pressure responses are more similar to controls (C84-C85) than in HIF-2α mutants.

results.result: Epidermal HIF-α deletions do not affect basal ventilation, acute hypoxic ventilatory response, blood oxygen saturation during hypoxia, or carotid body morphology, indicating that the cardiovascular phenotypes are not secondary to altered respiratory control.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 describe important negative controls supported by plethysmography data (Figure 8A-C) and histology (Figure 8D-G). These results exclude alternative explanations involving altered central chemoreception or respiratory drive. The carotid body analysis is particularly important given that K14 promoter might have off-target effects. However, the manuscript does not specify whether K14 is expressed in carotid body cells, which would strengthen this control.

results.result: This study demonstrates for the first time that oxygen sensing in a peripheral tissue (skin) directly modifies systemic cardiovascular responses to hypoxia through HIF-dependent mechanisms, establishing that cardiovascular adaptation represents a summation of responses across multiple tissues rather than solely central control.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C20-C21, C108, and C121-C122 represent the major conceptual advance of the study. The tissue-specific genetic approach combined with comprehensive physiological monitoring provides strong evidence that peripheral vascular beds actively shape systemic responses. The novelty claims (C3, C108) are justified given the limitations of prior work (C17, C96-C97). However, the mechanisms linking local skin responses to systemic effects (neural vs. humoral) remain incompletely defined.

results.result: The authors propose a model where HIF-1α promotes vasodilation via NOS2/NO while HIF-2α promotes vasoconstriction via arginase-mediated L-arginine depletion, with these opposing pathways modulating peripheral resistance, systemic blood pressure, and whole-body metabolism/behavior during hypoxic stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C105-C107, C109-C116, and C119 describe a mechanistic model supported by the genetic and physiological data. The opposing roles of HIF-1α and HIF-2α are well-documented across multiple mutants. The model is consistent with prior work (C105-C107, C109-C110) and current findings. However, the model remains somewhat speculative (C48 includes SPECULATION evidence type) as direct measurements of local NO levels during hypoxia in different mutants are limited, and the relative contributions of neural vs. paracrine mechanisms are unclear.

results.result: All four epidermal mutant lines show increased oxygen consumption during hypoxic acclimation, but only HIF-2α and Arg1 mutants preserve physical activity better than wild-type animals, suggesting peripheral vascular responses can modulate behavioral responses to environmental stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 describe metabolic and behavioral phenotypes supported by data in Figures 3-7. The dissociation between oxygen consumption (similar across genotypes) and activity (preserved only in HIF-2α and Arg1 mutants) is interesting and suggests complex interactions. However, the causal relationship between peripheral vascular changes and behavior (C119) remains correlative rather than mechanistic.

results.result: The mouse data are consistent with human studies showing that patients with germline HIF-2α gain-of-function mutations have elevated baseline heart rate and enhanced cardiac responses to hypoxia.
results.evaluation: Claim C120 draws a parallel between the current mouse data and human genetic studies. The comparison is reasonable given that HIF-2α loss-of-function in mice shows opposite effects (preserved heart rate) to gain-of-function in humans (elevated heart rate). However, the human mutations are systemic while the mouse deletions are epidermal-specific, limiting direct comparability.

results.result: This study represents the first detailed investigation of cardiovascular acclimation to hypoxia in mice over intermediate timeframes (48-72 hours) using radiotelemetry in unanesthetized animals, addressing a gap between acute studies (<10 min, anesthetized) and chronic studies (weeks-months).
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 and C17-C18 describe the novelty of the experimental approach. The characterization of prior literature appears accurate based on citations provided. The use of radiotelemetry in conscious animals over 48-72 hours does represent a methodological advance. However, the claim of being 'first' (C96) should be tempered as some prior studies may have used similar timeframes.

results.result: The study used extensively backcrossed C57/Bl6J mice with keratinocyte-specific gene deletions driven by the K14 promoter. The NOS2 conditional allele was generated by flanking exon 3 with loxP sites. Statistical analysis using non-linear regression with AICc showed >99.99% probability that mutant and control data are best represented by separate models.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 describe methodological details. The genetic background control (C123) and K14 promoter specificity (C124) are appropriate. The NOS2 allele design (C125-C126) is standard. The statistical approach (C127) using AICc for model comparison is rigorous and the >99.99% probability threshold is very stringent. However, the manuscript lacks some details on sample size calculations and whether investigators were blinded.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on cardiovascular regulation, skin biology, hypoxic responses across species, HIF transcription factor function, and the role of NO in vascular control, drawing on established literature and the authors' prior work.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C4-C16, C103-C104 represent background knowledge and prior work appropriately cited throughout. These establish the scientific context but are not novel findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization of prior work seems accurate, though detailed verification of all cited claims is beyond the scope of this review.
